# British Agricultural Revolution

The British Agricultural Revolution was a transformation in English agricultural output and productivity in the century after 1750, achieved through changes in farming practice, and accompanied by a transformation of the agrarian economy and society, including marketing, landholding, field systems, property rights, enclosure, and social relations. 1 Its size, timing, and even its existence as a distinct "revolution" are actively disputed among economic historians.

| Key fact | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Output growth | English agricultural output rose 2.5 to 3 times from 1700 to 1850, and more than doubled in the century after 1750 2 |
| Wheat yields | Average yields rose above 18 bushels per acre by 1800 and toward 30 bushels by the mid-nineteenth century, breaking a medieval ceiling of about 18 to 20 bushels 2 |
| Labour | By 1800 England was unique in having only about 30 to 35 percent of its workforce in agriculture 2 |
| Enclosure effect | Instrumental-variable estimates put the yield gain from Parliamentary enclosure at 45 percent, against older claims that enclosure made only a minor contribution 3 • 4 |
| Nitrogen mechanism | Nitrogen-fixing plants such as clover and turnips accounted for about half of the long-run rise in grain yields 5 |
| Growth rates | Estimated productivity growth of 2 percent per decade between 1600 and 1800, rising to 5 percent per decade between 1810 and 1860 6 |
| Distribution | Parliamentary enclosure raised the Gini coefficient of plot values by 22 percentage points on a mean of 0.74 3 |

## What the revolution comprised

Mark Overton dates the agricultural revolution to the century after 1750 and describes it as two linked transformations. The first was a transformation in output and productivity brought about by changes in farming practice; the second was a transformation of the agrarian economy and society, including marketing, landholding, field systems, property rights, enclosure, and social relations. 1 The dating of the whole process varies widely by author: Prothero dated it 1760 to 1830, Chambers and Mingay 1750 to 1880, Kerridge 1560 to 1767, Jones 1649 to 1688, and Thompson two separate revolutions, 1660 to 1750 and 1815 to 1880. 7 

Gradual or concentrated? The evidence points to gradualism with a late acceleration. Wheat yields did not break through the medieval ceiling of around 18 to 20 bushels per acre until the early to mid-eighteenth century, and population, which rose above 5.5 million in the late 1730s, kept rising thereafter. 2 A 2025 Quarterly Journal of Economics study finds English productivity growth was zero before 1600 and began around 1600, almost a century before the Glorious Revolution. 6 Annual estimates likewise place the start of a continuous upward trend in both labor productivity and output per unit of land in the early eighteenth century. 8 At the other end, a review of farm-record wheat yields, showing 19 bushels per acre in the 1720s, 21 to 22 by the mid-eighteenth century, a dip in the 1780s and 1790s, a peak near 30 bushels in the 1840s, and a plateau of 27 to 28 thereafter, places the revolution "firmly within the period from about 1800 to 1850". 9 

## By the numbers

Overton's summary figures for 1700 to 1850 are output up by some 170 to 180 percent on a total farm area risen by only one third, land productivity rather more than doubled with the larger part of the increase after 1800, cereal yields up two and a half times, and labor productivity roughly doubled. 10 His own journal article gives output growth of between 2.5 and 3 times from 1700 to 1850. 2 

These magnitudes are contested. A revisionist study using four separate tests argues that the traditional claim of a fourfold growth of farm output and output per farm worker between 1270/1300 and 1870 must be wrong, and that growth was much more limited. 11 A Birmingham working paper using rents, prices, wages, and capital costs for 1690 to 1914 estimates profit-augmentation of 0.4 percent per year and output- and input-based total factor productivity growth of 0.1 and 0.2 percent, which reads as steady progress rather than revolutionary change. 7 The 2025 QJE estimates of 2 percent per decade before 1800 and 5 percent per decade from 1810 to 1860 sit between these poles. 6 

## Techniques and their measured effects

Seed drilling and horse-hoeing. A counterfactual analysis of Arthur Young's farm-level data for around 1770 finds that English wheat yields could have been 51 percent higher had the best available techniques been fully adopted. Seed drilling and horse-hoeing account for 70 percent of that postulated increase, some 9 bushels per acre, because adoption could rise from 8 percent to 100 percent and the per-acre effect was large; the Norfolk four-course rotation contributes 13 percent, harvesting turnips 4 percent, and under-drainage 2 percent. 12 A related Journal of Economic History study of c.1770 yields confirms that while drainage and marling helped, the eighteenth-century innovations, particularly turnips and seed drills, were much more effective. 13 Drill adoption rose steadily after 1810, became widespread in the 1840s "Age of High Farming", and reached 50 percent by 1870, which would have raised mean yields from 23 to 27 bushels, close to the actual 1870 yield of around 28. 12 

The nitrogen mechanism. Turnips and clover mattered biologically as well as agronomically. A biological model of nitrogen flows finds that nitrogen-fixing plants accounted for about half of the rise in English grain yields from the middle ages to the industrial revolution, with the rest from better cultivation, seeds, and drainage. 5 In Norfolk, clover and turnips, not grown at all previously, occupied 9 percent of the sown area in 1660 to 1739 and 49 percent by 1836. 2 A 2024 Cliometrica study of 1645 to 1740 attributes about half of the variation in grain yields to nitrogen-fixing plants, better cultivation, and improved seeds, with the remainder to changing climatic conditions. 14 The same nitrogen chemistry explains the revolution's pace: because nitrogen release was slow, the English revolution was necessarily much more gradual than the twentieth-century Green Revolution, which supplied fixed nitrogen industrially. 5 

## Enclosure: productivity and dispossession

On one side, a study using the entire population of English Parliamentary enclosure acts between 1750 and 1830 finds, using an instrumental variable, that Parliamentary enclosure raised agricultural yield by 45 percent, a gain not driven by substitution between activities. 3 Contemporary Board of Agriculture "General Views" point the same way: wheat yields rose 66 percent and 29 percent in two Bedfordshire parishes and 150 percent at Barton, Lincolnshire, and averaged 66 percent across all reports with before-and-after figures. 3 On the other side, R.C. Allen finds that enclosure made only a minor contribution to the doubling of crop yields and labor productivity between the middle ages and the nineteenth century: in the light arable district around 1800, yields in open and enclosed villages were identical; in the pasture district enclosed yields were perhaps a tenth higher; in the heavy arable district about a quarter higher. 4 A case study of Canwick, Lincolnshire, sits between them: after enclosure wheat yields rose only 10 percent, but barley and oats rose 40 and 78 percent, and sheep numbers rose 33 percent while the value of their output rose 590 percent. 2 Allen does concede that enclosure greatly accelerated adoption of the Norfolk rotation and drainage investment, while showing that open-field villages were not impervious to new techniques. 4 

Redistribution was real regardless. The same NBER study finds Parliamentary enclosure increased the Gini coefficient of the value of land plots in an enclosing parish by 22 percentage points relative to a mean of 0.74. 3 Allen argues that if enclosure contributed little to productivity, the large rent increases it produced represented a redistribution of income from farmers to landlords. 4 The extent of enclosure also predates the Parliamentary era: one estimate suggests perhaps 45 percent of England was enclosed by 1550 and 75 percent by 1760, with a further 19 percent enclosed by Acts of Parliament between 1760 and 1914. 15 On the social side, most laboring households in the arable lowlands of southern and eastern England were already thoroughly proletarian before parliamentary enclosure, and Lavrovsky found the independent peasantry had already ceased to exist even in unenclosed parishes by the end of the eighteenth century, so enclosure was not the final stage in the making of an agrarian proletariat. 16 

## Key figures and myth-making

Overton argued in 1986 that the contributions of Jethro Tull, credited with the seed drill of 1701, and Thomas Coke, credited with the Norfolk rotation, have been overblown. 7 The quantitative work supports this deflation: drilling and horse-hoeing mattered most in the counterfactual, but the technique's actual adoption was only 8 percent around 1770 and reached 50 percent only by 1870. 12 Livestock improvement fits a different chronology: the review evidence places the main advances in livestock productivity in the hundred years following 1660. 10 

## Agriculture and the Industrial Revolution

The classic thesis holds that rising agricultural productivity released labor and food for industry. By 1800 England was unique in the world in having only about 30 to 35 percent of its workforce in agriculture, and by 1700 only around 48 percent, making England a historical exception at that time. 2 • 14 The NBER enclosure study links Parliamentary enclosures to increased innovation, improved farming practices and infrastructure, and a shift of labor out of agriculture toward industry, with released labor flowing primarily to the northern industrializing regions. 3 

Gregory Clark dissents: his estimates show that the growing population of Industrial Revolution England was fed mainly through food imports and through switching agricultural output toward food, not through an agricultural revolution, and he argues that output growth estimates for the 1760s to 1860s need substantial downward revision. 17 On wages, the 2025 QJE study explains the stagnant real wages of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, the period known as Engels' Pause, by rapid population growth putting downward pressure on wages rather than by absent productivity growth. 6 

## Comparisons: France and the Green Revolution

Clark's estimates also show that English agricultural productivity growth between 1500 and 1789 was no greater than the rates Philip Hoffman finds for the Paris Basin, and that before 1869 productivity growth came overwhelmingly from growing yields rather than labor productivity. 17 Revisionist comparative scholarship likewise questions the importance of enclosure and the expropriation of the small farmer as the key to Britain's divergence from France, pointing instead to the introduction of clover and multi-course rotations within a broader transformation. 18 Against the twentieth-century Green Revolution, the contrast is one of speed: nitrogen's chemistry made the English revolution gradual, where industrial fertilizer allowed rapid yield gains. 5
